opus-5.5.text:
I think a real product is one where the customer pays for it because it does a job, not because it's a demo, a research platform, or something to put on display in a lobby. In the past couple of years there have been a lot of impressive videos: robots doing backflips, folding clothes, dancing at galas. Those show progress in the technology, but they aren't products yet. Usually what you see is a carefully chosen clip, sometimes teleoperated, sometimes the best result out of many tries, in a fixed environment.

For me there are a few tests. First, it has to work autonomously, without a person behind it holding a joystick. Second, it has to be reliable. The success rate can't be 70 or 80 percent. In a real store, factory, or pharmacy, if a robot fails one out of every five times, someone has to stand next to it, and then the economics don't work. You need something like 99 percent or more on the tasks it's responsible for. Third, it has to generalize within its scenario. The products change, the lighting changes, the shelf layout changes, and it should still work without engineers coming on site to retune it. Fourth, the unit economics have to make sense. The cost of the robot plus maintenance has to be lower than the value of the labor it replaces, over a reasonable payback period.

So I'm fairly pragmatic about this. I don't think the first real products will be the general-purpose humanoid that does everything in your home. That's the long-term dream, and I share it. But the first real products are more likely to be in relatively structured commercial settings, like retail, warehousing, or pharmacies, where the main task is picking and placing many different kinds of items. Those tasks are valuable, they repeat at large scale, and they're now within reach of what our models can do reliably.

Once you have robots actually deployed and doing work every day, you get a flywheel. You get real data, find real failure cases, improve the model, and expand to the next scenario. I think that path, from a narrow but real product to more general capability, is how embodied intelligence actually becomes an industry rather than just a technology showcase.

r001.rationale: The response says a real product must do a job and that its cost and maintenance must be lower than the value of the labor it replaces, making productive value a requirement.

r002.rationale: It does not say a product may provide only a partial solution with humans covering tasks the robot cannot do; instead, it emphasizes autonomy without a person behind a joystick.

r003.rationale: It does not define productivity by comparing the robot’s work output per unit of time with a person’s.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is: a real product is something a customer pays for, uses every day, and would be upset to lose. That sounds trivial, but in embodied intelligence most of what gets called a "product" fails that test.

Let me be more specific. There are three things I look at.

First, does it close a loop in a real environment, not a lab? A demo where a robot folds a towel on a table that we set up ourselves is not a product. A product has to deal with the environment it was not trained on: a different kitchen, a different lighting condition, a different person walking past. If the system only works when we control the scene, it is a research result, and research results are valuable, but we should call them what they are.

Second, is the task defined by the customer or by us? A lot of teams pick tasks because they are easy to show, not because anyone needs them. When I talk to factory owners or logistics operators, the things they actually want are often boring: pick this object from this bin, put it there, do it ten hours a day, do not break anything. If the robot does that reliably, nobody cares whether it looks impressive on video. That reliability, say ninety-nine point something percent over thousands of cycles, is the whole product.

Third, is there a path to repeatable deployment? A product has to be the same thing deployed the second time, the tenth time, the hundredth time, without a team of engineers living on site. That means the model has to generalize enough that integration cost drops with each deployment rather than staying flat. For me that is the core reason to work on general-purpose embodied models at all. The point is not to make a humanoid look human. The point is to make the marginal cost of a new deployment go toward zero.

So in the current stage, I would say real products in this industry are still mostly narrow: specific manipulation tasks in structured or semi-structured settings, some mobile tasks, some inspection. The general-purpose robot that walks into any home and helps is still a goal, not a product. And I think it is important for people in this field, myself included, to be honest about that distinction, because the gap between a great demo and a product that survives contact with reality is where most of the actual work is.

r001.rationale: The response emphasizes customer use, reliability, and repeatable deployment, but does not identify creating productivity as a necessary condition.

r002.rationale: It does not say a product may qualify while humans perform work the robot cannot do.

r003.rationale: It mentions reliability over many cycles, but gives no criterion comparing the robot’s output per unit time with a person’s.

astra-6.text:
I think a real product has to complete a useful task reliably in the environment where a customer actually needs it. A robot that performs impressively in a demo is a technical achievement, but there’s still a gap between that and a product.

The key question is whether someone will keep paying to use it. Does it save them time, reduce costs, or do something they couldn’t do before? And can it deliver that value once you account for deployment, maintenance, and human intervention?

For embodied intelligence, the physical world makes this especially demanding. Conditions change, objects move, and unexpected situations happen. You don’t necessarily need a robot that can do everything. You need a clearly defined task that it can do consistently, with a sensible way to handle failures. That’s where I would draw the line between a demonstration and a real product.

r001.rationale: The candidate asks whether the product saves time or reduces costs, but does not make creating productivity a necessary condition; it also offers other possible sources of value.

r002.rationale: It says a robot need not do everything and should handle failures sensibly, but does not state that humans can cover work the robot cannot perform.

r003.rationale: The candidate gives no comparison between a robot’s output per unit of time and a person’s.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a real product has to complete a useful task reliably in a real environment, at a cost someone is willing to pay. For embodied intelligence, that means looking beyond whether a robot can perform an impressive demonstration. Can it do the job repeatedly? How often does a person need to intervene? What does deployment and maintenance cost?

A customer is buying an outcome. If the robot can consistently deliver that outcome and the economics work, then you have a product. If it only works under carefully prepared conditions with engineers standing nearby, I would still call it a prototype.

r001.rationale: The response makes reliably completing a useful task and delivering a customer outcome conditions for being a product, which communicates productivity as necessary.

r002.rationale: It mentions how often a person must intervene, but does not say a product may qualify when humans cover work the robot cannot perform.

r003.rationale: It discusses reliable task completion but does not define productivity by comparing the robot’s output per unit of time with a person’s.
